newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Israel says S.Africa-Syria deal threatens peace.
newsitem.headline: Israel says S.Africa-Syria deal threatens peace.

text.p: South Africa's proposed sale of weaponry to Syria comes at a bad time for the Middle East peace process and will upset the military balance if it goes ahead, Israel's ambassador to South Africa said on Tuesday.

Victor Harel said Israel had not been consulted about the plan to sell tank-gun targeting equipment to the Syrians, which has provoked an unusually strong warning from the United States, including a threat to cut off U.S. aid to South Africa.
"We cannot turn a blind eye. On the contrary, we are very very much concerned," Harel told Reuters. "This is the type of sale that, if it goes ahead, would destabilise the region completely.

"It comes at a very delicate time for the peace process and a very hopeful time since I believe we are on the eve of the signing of the Hebron agreement. And from there we would like to go on with the Palestinians and on with the Syrians. Therefore I think this comes at a very, very bad time for the peace process," Harel said.

After the proposed arms deal came to light on Sunday, leaked by unknown sources to a newspaper, South Africa had assured Israel that relations remained friendly and the proposed Syrian deal signalled no kind of change, the ambassador added.
"But if the sale goes ahead, surely it will put a burden on bilateral relations, because it will be providing sophisticated weapons to a country still almost in a state of war with Israel," he said.

Asked whether he believed the proposed sale was motivated by money or by ideology, Harel said: "We see the figures and we are talking about a huge amount of money. But obviously money is not everything. We are talking about a very complex region with many interests involved."

In a statement rejecting domestic and international criticism of the proposed deal, President Nelson Mandela's ruling African National Congress said that in the past South Africa favoured Israel and discriminated against Arab states.

Critics of the weapons deal with Syria were trying to reimpose pro-Israeli policies from the apartheid era "in order to prevent the conclusion of a just, even-handed and lasting peace" in the Middle East, the party said.

The row escalated on Tuesday when an aide to President Mandela accused Washington of high-handed bullying. One South African analyst shared that view, saying it would not be the first time that the Americans had tried to curb South Africa's high-tech arms export potential.

The three billion rand ($641 million) tank fire control system contract has yet to be finalised, but a U.S. spokesman said Washington had known about it for some time and had been discussing it with South Africa -- evidently with little impact.
The U.S. state department said on Monday "it would be extremely serious" if the sale went ahead.
The deal is said to involve an upgrade to the targeting capacity of Syria's Soviet-built T-72 tanks. The South African cabinet is due to decide later this month if it will go ahead.
Harel said Israel was "using diplomatic channels to try and reach the highest levels (in the South African government) in order to explain as friends our deep concerns".
"We do have time and we do find openness," he said.
